kaigo-atomic-risk-observation.heading: Observe risks and share near misses
paragraphs: In observation, distinguish words and behavior learned through interactions with the person from information actually measured, such as temperature or blood pressure. Noticing a difference from usual does not establish its cause. Do not record a feeling of heat to the touch as a measured body temperature.

Loose footwear, long hems, wet floors, cords in routes and faulty equipment present different hazards. An action possible yesterday may be difficult in today’s condition. Consider risks not only in walking but also movement while seated or lying and transfers between beds and equipment. Do not make uniform judgments based only on age or a disability label.

Risk management means anticipating hazards and preparing to prevent accidents. Record and share facts about near misses even when nobody is injured. Separate what happened and where, confirmed contributing factors and unconfirmed causes, and review responses and recurrence prevention as a team. Do not wait until harm occurs before learning.

Another learning example: a wheelchair moved before a transfer. If inspection confirms that the brakes were not applied, record that fact and share how to check before the next task. If the cause has not yet been investigated, report that the wheelchair moved and what remains to be checked rather than deciding in advance that the brakes caused it.

健康（けんこう） refers to health overall; 体調（たいちょう） to physical condition at a particular time; and 顔色（かおいろ） to facial color or appearance. Vital signs are indicators related to life and condition, such as temperature, breathing, pulse and blood pressure. Looking at facial color differs from measuring a value; planning a measurement differs from having completed it.

吐き気（はきけ） means feeling as if you may vomit; 嘔吐（おうと） means actually vomiting. 発汗（はっかん） means sweating; 発熱（はつねつ） refers to body temperature higher than usual. A picture of sweat being wiped away does not provide a temperature reading. はれる describes swelling, while むくむ describes edema. In reports, state the location and change specifically.

拘縮（こうしゅく）, contracture, is a condition in which a joint becomes difficult to move; distinguish it from briefly tensing a muscle. 褥瘡（じょくそう）, a pressure injury, involves skin or tissue damage associated with pressure and other factors; it is not limited to people confined to bed. 熱中症（ねっちゅうしょう）, heat illness, and heat shock from sudden temperature differences, such as during bathing, are not the same. Learn the terms here without independently deciding diagnoses or treatment.

痛い（いたい） expresses pain. 苦しい（くるしい） can mean difficulty breathing or other distress, depending on context. 症状（しょうじょう） means a manifestation of a condition; 発作（ほっさ） describes an episode in which symptoms appear suddenly. When you hear terms such as 咳（せき）, cough, dizziness or numbness, communicate the person’s words and what is known. A vocabulary label alone does not establish a disease.

Actual observations and responses follow the person’s condition, individual plan and facility procedures. Communicate changes and hazards to the necessary recipients. Do not try unfamiliar techniques from text alone.

kaigo-atomic-infection-chain.heading: The infection chain and task-appropriate protective equipment
paragraphs: Pathogens causing infectious disease include bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites. Report differences from usual, such as fever, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, rash or facial-color changes, to healthcare professionals. Symptoms alone do not identify a pathogen, and looking healthy does not mean infection is impossible.

Think in terms of the chain connecting an infection source, transmission route and susceptible host. Materials containing pathogens may be sources, while hands, objects and food may be involved in transmission. Hosts include people and animals. Reducing sources, interrupting transmission and supporting health serve different purposes. You do not need to wait until all three measures are available before taking those you can.

The textbook lists norovirus and O157 as contact-transmission examples, influenza as a droplet example, and tuberculosis and measles as airborne examples. These categories help explain routes. Do not assume one type of precaution is enough for a pathogen. Check actual methods against the pathogen, task and current facility guidance.

Standard precautions are not restricted to people with a diagnosis. Consider task-related risks involving contact with blood, saliva, nasal discharge, vomit, urine, feces, broken skin or mucous membranes. Select the necessary gloves, mask, apron or gown, and eye protection; do not use an identical set for every task.

Use gloves for risks of hand contact, aprons and similar items for clothing contamination, and goggles and similar items for splashes to the eyes. Caps also appear among the textbook’s supplies, but that does not mean everyone always needs them. Wear a mask over the nose, mouth and chin according to product instructions. Wearing one does not justify omitting other precautions.

Change disposable gloves according to procedures, including when changing the person or care task and when moving from dirty to clean work. Do not use one pair consecutively for several people. When removing them, enclose contaminated surfaces inward, discard them in the designated place and perform hand hygiene afterward. Gloves do not replace handwashing.

Communal living increases opportunities for contact, so prevent infection from entering, leaving and spreading within the facility. Combine hand hygiene, proper handling of supplies and the environment, and staff coordination according to facility procedures. People with reduced resistance need consideration, but healthy-looking people do not become exempt from precautions.

This learning checks understanding of infection mechanisms and judgments. Confirm putting on and removing protective equipment, contaminated-material handling, and disinfectant products, concentrations and contact times through facility training and guidance. Do not derive new handling procedures or diagnoses from this text.

kaigo-atomic-hand-coverage.heading: Hand hygiene: commonly missed areas of both hands
paragraphs: Thoroughly rubbing the palms does not prove that the backs of the hands, between fingers, thumbs, fingertips, around nails and wrists have also been covered. Check both hands. Awareness of hand areas helps avoid concluding ‘there is foam, so I am finished’ while leaving dirt behind.

With running water and liquid soap, consider the entire process: wetting, lathering and washing necessary areas, rinsing thoroughly, and drying with suitable paper towels or similar materials. Areas covered by watches and rings are hard to wash, so prepare beforehand according to facility rules. Washing only around jewelry is not always sufficient.

For broad surfaces, rub palms together, then use one palm to wash the back of the opposite hand and switch sides. Interlace fingers to reach between them and avoid missing the backs of the fingers. Check that care has not ended with the dominant hand alone.

Understand the textbook movements of enclosing a thumb in the opposite hand with a rotational action and placing fingertips and nail areas against the opposite palm. Switch sides and give wrists separate attention. Use the actual sequence and force learned in facility training.

When using an appropriate hand rub, take the product-specified amount, spread it over all areas and rub until dry. Cupping a hand helps receive the liquid, but check product instructions to establish whether the amount is appropriate. This method does not involve rinsing with water or wiping the product away midway.

For visible dirt, do not rely on an alcohol product alone: remove dirt with liquid soap and running water. Necessary methods may also differ by pathogen and task, so check facility guidance. Do not treat handwashing and hand rubbing as identical actions that automatically replace each other.

Touching a contaminated surface afterward can contaminate hands again. Check locations and handling order for clean and used items too. Knowing a diagram’s sequence of areas is separate from proving both hands were adequately treated in practice; verify technique through direct training.

kaigo-atomic-body-mechanics.heading: Conditions that reduce back strain and support worker health
paragraphs: Body mechanics considers how bones, joints, muscles and other structures coordinate movement. In assistance, its purpose is to protect the person and reduce the worker’s effort and lower-back burden. One posture diagram does not guarantee safe transfers for every person.

The base of support is the area enclosed by contact points supporting the body. Principles include appropriately spacing the feet and lowering the center of gravity. A properly used cane’s contact point changes the supporting area, but that alone does not prevent every fall. Consider the person, equipment and floor together.

Bringing the working area close to the body and using large muscle groups such as the legs and buttocks helps avoid concentrating strain on the lower back alone. Avoid lifting a person with straight knees using only the back or twisting the lower back under load. Reposition the feet to turn the body toward the direction of movement.

Other principles include bringing limbs together as feasible, moving the center of gravity horizontally, using whole-body movement and considering a lever’s fulcrum and force direction. Distance from the fulcrum changes how force acts, but knowledge alone does not determine where to use the body as a fulcrum. Do not bind joints or bend them into pain to create a posture.

Do not reinterpret the textbook’s ‘pulling’ as dragging skin against bedding or pulling the affected arm. Horizontal movement using friction-reducing equipment differs from directly dragging the body. Check skin, pain, personal abilities and equipment conditions.

Use the person’s abilities and consider equipment such as lifts, slide sheets and transfer boards, together with coordination between trained workers. For someone needing full transfer assistance, correct posture does not authorize lifting them alone. Prioritize checking suitable equipment and methods rather than relying on manual lifting. Distinguish sheets from boards: similar names do not make their fit or use identical.

Workers’ own meals and nutrition, sleep, manageable exercise and rest also matter. Make time for meals and sleep and maintain a daily rhythm. Do not carry worries alone: consult colleagues or more experienced staff and consider stress-management approaches that suit you. Report illness or excessive strain, and adjust support conditions rather than continuing unreasonable work.

This unit teaches principles and checks of working conditions. Actual transfers and repositioning require assessment of the person, an individual plan, equipment instructions and practical training. Spacing your feet or memorizing principles alone does not justify trying an unfamiliar operation.

kaigo-atomic-disaster.heading: Prepare for disasters: connect supplies, responsibilities and communication
paragraphs: Earthquakes, typhoons and fires present different hazards. Routinely check the facility’s disaster-response plan, evacuation routes, communication methods and community cooperation arrangements. Share who will help whom beforehand rather than deciding roles only after a disaster occurs.

Emergency supplies may include water and food, personally needed medicines and medical supplies, first-aid supplies, lights, a radio and batteries, warmth, clothing, hygiene supplies and head protection. Also check preparations for valuables such as cash and necessary documents according to personal needs and facility management methods. These are examples for organizing preparation, not identical quantities or items for everyone. Check the plan, expiry dates and actual needs; the textbook picture is not a complete inventory.

Drills check assistance if normal routes cannot be used, responsibility for people needing mobility help and alternatives if communication fails. Record the actual places, people and conditions checked. Packing supplies in a bag and completing evacuation are separate outcomes.

For people using powered medical equipment such as oxygen concentrators, consult healthcare professionals and the equipment provider beforehand about who will make contact during an outage and how necessary support, backup equipment or power will be secured. Preparation must fit the person’s equipment and plan; this learning does not authorize workers to decide connections or oxygen flow rates.

Learning example: a supply list exists, but nobody is assigned to support a person receiving oxygen therapy during a power outage. Do not regard the list alone as completed preparation. Check responsibilities, contacts, equipment-related preparations and the movement plan with those involved. Having equipment and having an arrangement that can actually use it are different.

kaigo-atomic-communication.heading: Two-way communication and choosing questions
paragraphs: Communication is a mutual exchange of thoughts, feelings and information in which understanding is checked. Speaker and listener roles are not fixed: both people send and receive messages. A worker saying everything they intended does not prove that the other person understood.

Speech, writing and sign language use language. Do not treat sign language as merely arbitrary hand gestures. Facial expressions, posture, gaze and gestures, meanwhile, are nonverbal cues. Check these as well as words in ways suited to the person.

Active listening means listening attentively and accurately; empathy means trying to understand feelings from the other person’s perspective; acceptance means acknowledging their feelings and views. These related concepts have different purposes. They do not mean steering the person toward the conclusion the worker considers correct.

Closed questions answerable with yes/no or limited choices help confirm specifics. Open questions allow the person to discuss thoughts and wishes more broadly. However, using only closed questions can make an exchange one-sided, while repeatedly asking ‘why’ even in open questions may feel accusatory. Choose questions suited to the purpose and the burden on the person.

Values are influenced by the period and environment in which someone grew up and their experiences. Respect feelings and views, and speak courteously as one adult to another. Check meaning as needed with family and other professionals as well as the person receiving care, to support trustworthy care.

Learning example: repeatedly asking someone who does not want to attend an event ‘Why aren’t you going?’ is not appropriate merely because it is an open question. Pause the questions, listen to what they want to say and, if necessary, use brief checks to confirm choices. Question format alone does not guarantee a good exchange.

kaigo-atomic-listening-consent.heading: From active listening to explanation, understanding and consent
paragraphs: Repeating the key points of the person’s words shows that you are listening and helps identify misunderstandings. Preserve when something happened, which body area was involved and how the person felt; do not rephrase their account into the worker’s conclusion. Do not report something described as ‘since yesterday’ as having begun today.

Face the person and adjust eye level, speaking speed, a calm voice and pauses. Crossed arms or leaning far away can give an impression of not listening. However, meanings of gaze and gestures vary between people and cultures. Do not impose identical eye contact or posture on everyone.

How conversational distance and physical touch are received also depends on the person, situation, manner, force and frequency. Do not assume holding hands conveys warmth to everyone. Check how the person wants to interact. General cultural tendencies do not replace personal wishes.

Present assistance options and explain each option’s benefits and disadvantages in a way the person can understand. Support them to think, choose and express a decision, and respect that decision. Merely explaining the purpose does not establish consent.

Learning example: disadvantages have not yet been explained, but the person nods and the worker plans to record ‘understood everything and consented.’ A nod alone does not prove complete understanding. Supply the necessary information and check understanding and the actual choice. Consent relates to the scope of assistance explained.

This learning practices communication and checking. Actual assistance follows the person’s condition, plan and facility procedures. Do not record unconfirmed consent or assistance not yet provided as complete.

120.title: Observe risks and share near misses
objectives: Separate the person’s words, observations and measurements, and record hazards and unconfirmed causes.
Share near misses without injury and use terms accurately to support recurrence prevention.
120.context: Learn to observe hazards and communicate causes that remain unknown. The terminology list is a reference, not an assignment to learn every term anew at once.
120.artCaption: Workers review a situation together. Share events without injury too, and describe causes only to the extent confirmed.

121.title: The infection chain and task-appropriate protective equipment
objectives: Distinguish infection sources, routes and hosts, and explain precautions needed before diagnosis.
Select protective equipment for task risks and distinguish glove changes from hand hygiene.
121.context: Knowledge learning about transmission routes and supply selection. It does not involve handling practice or mixing disinfectants.
121.artCaption: A scene checking task-appropriate protective equipment. The illustrated supplies are not an identical set to use for every task.

122.title: Hand hygiene: commonly missed areas of both hands
objectives: Distinguish running-water/soap washing from hand rubbing and check areas of both hands.
Consider visible dirt and renewed contact, and explain hand hygiene appropriate to products and the facility.
122.context: Check differences in areas and methods of hand hygiene. Reading these movement descriptions does not replace facility practical training.
122.artCaption: A scene washing hands under running water. The picture alone cannot confirm that every area was washed, rinsed and dried.

123.title: Conditions that reduce back strain and support worker health
objectives: Distinguish base-of-support, center-of-gravity, muscle-group and lever principles from permission to perform techniques.
Reduce strain by considering personal abilities, equipment, staffing and workers’ physical and mental health together.
123.context: Knowledge learning about combined assistance conditions rather than relying on posture alone. It does not involve practicing lifting people.
123.artCaption: A scene checking working conditions around an empty bed. It does not demonstrate lifting a person or establish practical safety.

124.title: Prepare for disasters: connect supplies, responsibilities and communication
objectives: Check disaster-specific hazards, supplies, roles and communication arrangements beforehand.
Connect individual needs such as medical equipment to the plan and distinguish preparation from completed evacuation.
124.context: Check responsibilities and individual needs rather than treating supply counts alone as complete preparation. It does not involve equipment operation or changing oxygen settings.
124.artCaption: A scene showing rest or consultation and preparations of disaster supplies. It does not establish individual responsibilities or completed evacuation.

125.title: Two-way communication and choosing questions
objectives: Distinguish verbal/nonverbal communication and listening/empathy/acceptance, and check mutual understanding.
Choose open and closed questions according to their purpose and the burden on the person.
125.context: Two-way learning focused on understanding what the person wants to convey rather than continuing to ask questions.
125.artCaption: A scene listening to the person and checking meaning. Question format alone does not establish understanding.

126.title: From active listening to explanation, understanding and consent
objectives: Adapt repetition, eye level, pauses and distance to the person and accurately check what was heard.
Explain benefits and disadvantages, and distinguish nodding from understanding, decisions and consent.
126.context: Distinguish what was said from what the person understood and chose, and check the scope of assistance.
126.artCaption: A scene explaining item locations or assistance. Understanding and consent require separate checks beyond simply speaking.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-risk-observatio.prompt: A wheelchair moved, but the person did not fall and was not injured. How should this near miss be handled?
options: Record the movement and confirmed conditions, and share unconfirmed aspects of the cause separately.
Omit observation and records if nobody is injured.
Record the brakes as the established cause even though they have not yet been inspected.
Do not discuss prevention until the next accident causes injury.
rationales: Share established facts even about events without injury and use them to prevent recurrence.
Near misses contain useful prevention information; absence of injury alone does not justify omitting them.
An assumption before inspection cannot be recorded as a confirmed cause.
Consider prevention based on this hazard rather than waiting for harm.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-infection-chain.prompt: A task involves contact with vomit from someone who does not yet have an infectious-disease diagnosis. Which approach is appropriate?
options: Without a diagnosis, bare-handed contact is acceptable.
If the person looks well, protective equipment and hand hygiene can be omitted.
Follow procedures for protective equipment and hand hygiene suited to the contact risk without waiting for a diagnosis.
Gloves remove the need for hand hygiene after taking them off.
rationales: Standard precautions are not determined solely by diagnosis; consider the risk of contact with vomit.
A healthy appearance is not grounds for omitting necessary infection precautions.
Check supplies and methods against task risks and take necessary precautions before diagnosis too.
Glove use and hand hygiene afterward are both necessary.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-hand-coverage.prompt: Both palms have been washed, but the thumbs and areas around the nails have not yet been reached. What is appropriate?
options: Treat unwashed areas as washed if there is plenty of foam.
Treat all necessary areas of both hands according to the method being used before finishing.
If one palm is clean, consider the other hand finished too.
Knowing the diagram’s sequence makes actual area checks unnecessary.
rationales: Foam quantity alone does not prove coverage of each area.
This checks necessary areas on both sides, including thumbs, fingertips and areas around nails.
Check the two hands and their areas separately.
Knowledge of a procedure differs from adequately carrying it out in practice.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-body-mechanics.prompt: A care worker stands with feet apart. Does that alone justify deciding they may lift every person single-handedly?
options: With feet apart, the person’s condition no longer needs checking.
Lowering the center of gravity removes the need for equipment.
Understanding a posture diagram permits transfers without practical training.
Posture alone is insufficient; check personal abilities, equipment, staffing and trained methods.
rationales: A worker’s foot spacing cannot replace assessment of the person’s condition and abilities.
Adjusting posture does not remove the need to consider suitable assistive equipment.
Understanding a diagram alone does not establish the ability to perform transfers safely.
This checks working conditions, including equipment and methods, rather than relying only on principles.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-disaster.prompt: Disaster supplies are ready, but nobody is assigned to support a person receiving oxygen therapy during a power outage. What is appropriate?
options: The supply list also completes the check of individual responsibilities.
Wait until a power outage to look for contacts for the first time.
Check responsibilities, communication, necessary preparations and the movement plan with healthcare professionals and the equipment provider.
The worker who gathered supplies independently decides the person’s oxygen settings.
rationales: Preparing supplies and confirming the support arrangement the person needs are separate matters.
Check roles and communication methods before a disaster to reduce confusion.
This checks an individual plan suited to the person and equipment with those involved.
This learning and supply preparation do not grant authority to decide medical-equipment settings independently.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-communication.prompt: Someone who does not want to attend an event is repeatedly asked ‘Why aren’t you going?’ What is an appropriate change?
options: Stop the pressuring questions, listen to what the person wants to say and use questions that do not overburden them to confirm wishes.
Keep asking the same question despite no reply because it is open-ended.
Avoid specific checks because all closed questions are bad.
Decide that the worker’s view is the person’s wish.
rationales: An open format alone does not make an exchange appropriate. Check the person’s wishes and the burden on them.
Repeated ‘why’ questions may feel accusatory and need adjustment.
Closed questions also help clarify choices or facts.
Do not replace listening to the person’s views with the worker’s decision.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-listening-conse.prompt: Disadvantages have not yet been explained, but the person nods and the worker plans to record ‘understood everything and consented.’ What is appropriate?
options: Omit the remaining explanation because the person nodded.
Treat an explanation of the purpose alone as consent to every assistance task.
Later record consent as already given for matters never explained.
Explain benefits and disadvantages understandably, and check understanding and the person’s choice.
rationales: One nod does not establish understanding of information that has not been explained.
Check explanation, consent and the scope of consent separately.
Do not invent consent to unexplained matters and record it as fact.
This supplies necessary information and supports the person to understand and express a decision.
